Date: 2025-06-25
Time: 14:00 PT

Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Rao (Redwood SE), Marcus Lee (Oceanic - Head of ML), Sofia Alvarez (Oceanic - Platform Eng), Ethan Park (Oceanic - SRE)
summary: Technical deep dive on prefix/prompt caching strategy. Covered cache key design, hit-rate expectations, tenant isolation and safety, TTLs, caching multi-turn chat, interaction with KV cache and batching, quantization effects, and VPC/on-prem constraints. Agreed next steps: run hit-rate sim, share prompt corpus, and pilot setup details.
topics: Prefix caching basics; cache keys & namespace; hit-rate modeling; multi-tenant safety and privacy; TTLs and eviction; interaction with KV cache & KV sharding; batching implications for latency/throughput; quantization compatibility; deployment modes (hosted vs dedicated vs vpc/on-prem); benchmarks and pilot plan.
transcript:
[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — should we do quick intros?
[00:06] Marcus Lee: Marcus here, head of ML at Oceanic. We're focused on real-time question answering over our oceanographic datasets, roughly 250 rps average but spikes to 1k.
[00:12] Sofia Alvarez: Sofia - platform engineer, I own infra and networking.
[00:16] Ethan Park: Ethan - SRE, I'll be involved on latency/ops side.
[00:19] Priya Rao: Priya from Redwood, I'm the SE, I'll run through technical details on prefix caching and KV interplay.
[00:25] Alex Chen: Quick agenda: prefix cache keys, hit rates, multi-tenant safety, batching impacts, and then deployment constraints for VPC/on-prem.
[00:33] Marcus Lee: high-level goal: reduce per-request latency and token cost for our chat sessions. We're seeing heavy repeated prefixes because our prompts include a 400-token system prompt plus common domain context, so hoping prefix caching buys us a lot.
[00:44] Priya Rao: yeah that's the common pattern. two main approaches: static prefix caching (cache the whole prefix key per customer/model/temperature) and more dynamic shardable kv-caching where cached KV states are reused as long as key matches, with versioning.
[00:58] Sofia Alvarez: can you clarify what you mean by cache key? do we need to hash entire prompt plus client id? concerned about PII leaking across tenants.
[01:05] Priya Rao: good Q. recommended key = hash(model + model_version + normalized_prefix + tenancy_namespace + quantization_profile + policy_flags). normalized_prefix means we canonicalize whitespace/tokenization and strip ephemeral runtime data. we also include a version tag so we can invalidate when we change system prompts.
[01:22] Marcus Lee: we have multi-tenant customers inside our app, so at Oceanic the tenant id is our customer org id; we'd want Redwood cache to be tenant-aware. we do not want cross-tenant hits.
[01:31] Alex Chen: absolutely—Redwood prefix cache is namespace-scoped by tenancy for Dedicated and Private. For hosted we support customer scoping but need to verify legal/consent for storing prefixes; for your pilot (Dedicated) we can guarantee strict isolation — different namespace, separate cache pools if desired.
[01:46] Ethan Park: what about shared caches for cost reasons? what's the tradeoff?
[01:50] Priya Rao: shared caches can increase hit-rates if tenants share similar prompts, but you'd need to strip tenant-specific tokens and be careful about PII. tradeoffs: higher hit-rate vs stricter data isolation. For enterprise we usually recommend per-tenant namespaces or tagging with encryption-at-rest and audit logs.
[02:05] Marcus Lee: ok, hit-rate modeling — how much can we realistically expect? our prefix is heavy because system + common context = ~400 tokens, user message is variable 20-80 tokens.
[02:15] Priya Rao: rough rule: if your prefixes are highly repetitive across sessions then hit-rate can be 40–70% for the prefix stage. actual savings depend on where tokens fall — caching prefix KV state lets you avoid re-computing attention for those tokens; for decoder-only models that can be 30–60% token cost reduction if cache hit. but if your user messages are unique and long, marginal savings drop.
[02:38] Sofia Alvarez: do we cache per-sequence or per-turn? i.e. for multi-turn chat, do we cache each conversation's prefix and each turn's KV?
[02:45] Priya Rao: we support both. typical pattern: cache the initial static prefix (system + few-shot examples) at global or tenant level, and then cache recent conversation prefixes at a per-session short TTL — say 5–30 minutes — because conversations mutate. The KV cache is append-only for the current session, we maintain per-session KV chains and can snapshot those for later reuse if the session is likely to recur.
[03:05] Marcus Lee: snapshotting sounds risky for privacy.
[03:08] Priya Rao: agreed, snapshotting only with explicit consent and you'd want those snapshots encrypted with your KMS. For Dedicated/Private we can wire KMS so Redwood never has access to keys.
[03:16] Ethan Park: what about TTLs and eviction? eviction causing cold-starts during high QPS bursts is a concern.
[03:21] Priya Rao: TTL strategy: keep long-lived static prefixes with TTLs of days to weeks, short-lived session prefixes with TTLs of minutes. eviction policy is LRU by default but you can pin items for dedicated pools. For bursts we support a warm-up mode where the system pre-populates cache entries for expected patterns — you provide sample inputs and we pre-warm.
[03:39] Alex Chen: there's also the option of reserving Dedicated capacity so your pool has higher cache retention because fewer tenants compete and memory is dedicated.
[03:47] Marcus Lee: how does caching interact with batching and throughput? if we hit cache we skip expensive compute, but does it affect how many requests we can batch?
[03:56] Priya Rao: good point. caching typically reduces per-request compute so you get higher throughput overall. However batching aims to aggregate token generation across concurrent requests — if many requests are cache hits, they short-circuit and don't enter the same generation batch, which can reduce batching efficiency but still improves latency. We optimize for hybrid: cached requests are fast path; non-cached requests get prioritized into batching windows. There's tunable policies for max wait (we default to 10–20ms) so your P95 latency isn't affected much.
[04:22] Sofia Alvarez: quantization — any incompatibilities? we run int8 quantized models on Dedicated nodes.
[04:27] Priya Rao: prefix caching is orthogonal to weight quantization; cache stores KV activations (float tensors) or quantized representations depending on runtime. our runtime supports storing KV in a quantized compressed format for memory savings, but that requires model-runtime compatibility. we tag cache entries with quantization_profile in the key so we won't serve a cached kv to a different quantization profile.
[04:47] Marcus Lee: can you describe the cache key collision risk? if we include many flags in the key, we might fragment hit-rate.
[04:53] Priya Rao: yeah you have to balance key entropy. rule of thumb: include only dimensions that change the decoding result: model+version, normalization, tenant namespace, temperature/stop-seq/presence of streaming. Avoid including ephemeral flags like request-id. We also provide a 'relaxed key' mode that omits low-impact flags to increase hit-rate at the cost of stricter reproducibility.
[05:13] Ethan Park: what's the overhead to compute hash and normalize? at 1k spikes, hashing could be a hotspot.
[05:18] Priya Rao: hashing is cheap (murmur3/xxhash) and done client-side in Redwood SDK optionally; normalization is where cost can be. We recommend SDK-side canonicalization so your infra can cache before calling Redwood; otherwise we do it at the edge which adds ~1–3ms.
[05:33] Marcus Lee: can we do a hybrid: SDK computes a key and sends both key+prefix so the server can verify?
[05:37] Priya Rao: yes, we support client-provided cache-key header with server-side verification. server will fall back to computed key if verification fails. This allows you to shard cache keys deterministically if you want.
[05:47] Alex Chen: security question — audit trails and retention?
[05:50] Priya Rao: every cache hit and miss is logged with key-hash (not raw prompt) and tenant id. For Dedicated/Private logs can be shipped to your SIEM and we support redaction. Retention policies configurable per-customer.
[06:02] Sofia Alvarez: VPC/on-prem constraints — if we run private with our KMS, do we still get cache dedup across nodes?
[06:08] Priya Rao: for on-prem or VPC we can run a cache cluster within your network; dedup across zones is possible with Redis-like distributed stores or sharded local caches. For strict air-gapped setups we recommend local caches co-located with inference nodes to avoid egress.
[06:22] Marcus Lee: what's the memory footprint? 400-token prefix KV state — approx how big per entry?
[06:28] Priya Rao: depends on model dims; for a 7B-like model with 4096 context and 4096-dim kv vectors, a single token's KV might be ~32 bytes? hmm approximate: per-token KV might be 64–128 bytes compressed; so 400 tokens ~25–50KB per entry in compressed quantized form. If you keep 100k entries, that's a few GBs. Exact numbers depend on quantization and compression.
[06:52] Ethan Park: we have a 256GB GPU host budget for cache memory — any ballpark for retention with that?
[06:58] Priya Rao: ballpark: with heavy compression you could store millions of tokens; but realistic per-entry sizes and metadata put you in hundreds of thousands of entries. we'll run numbers with your sample corpus.
[07:10] Marcus Lee: any safety concerns: prefix caching could accidentally return prior tenant data if namespace bug occurs — how do you mitigate?
[07:17] Priya Rao: several mitigations: namespace isolation by default, strict zero-copy policies between tenants in Dedicated, per-tenant cache shards, audit logs for cross-tenant access, and automatic integrity checks (we tag entries with tenant-hash and verify on retrieval). Also we recommend signing keys for cache entries when running in customer's VPC with their KMS.
[07:35] Sofia Alvarez: what's the failure mode if cached KV is incompatible with a new model update?
[07:40] Priya Rao: we version cache keys — model_version included — so after a model update old keys won't match. There's also a 'compatibility layer' for minor tokenizer or truncation changes but we prefer to invalidate explicitly to avoid subtle silent errors.
[07:53] Marcus Lee: can we evict/purge programmatically? e.g., if we rotate system prompt we want to invalidate a tenant's prefix entries.
[07:58] Priya Rao: yes, API to bulk-invalidate by tag/namespace and point-in-time invalidation. Also support for time-based rollouts.
[08:06] Alex Chen: measurement and benchmark section — what do we need from Oceanic to estimate real savings?
[08:11] Marcus Lee: we can provide a sample of 50k prompt pairs and traffic histogram across hours, plus token distributions.
[08:17] Priya Rao: perfect. Priya: we'll run a sim to estimate hit-rate and cost savings assuming different key-strategies (strict vs relaxed).
[08:25] Priya Rao: quick note on streaming and tool-calls: if you use function/tool-calling, we treat tool outputs as part of the conversation so cache keys should include presence/absence of tool calls; otherwise you risk hitting cached prefixes with missing tool outputs.
[08:39] Ethan Park: edge case: what if the prefix contains user-specific ephemeral tokens like timestamps — normalization must remove those.
[08:45] Priya Rao: yes, normalization pipeline strips high-variance tokens by default, but you can provide custom regex rules in SDK to scrub.
[08:52] Marcus Lee: curious about metrics: what dashboards do you expose?
[08:55] Priya Rao: Redwood Console shows per-namespace hit-rate, hit/miss latency, token-savings, cost-saved estimates, and per-key heatmap for top prefixes. We also export to Prometheus for alerting.
[09:07] Sofia Alvarez: on compliance: SOC2 and logs — how long do you keep raw prompts in Hosted?
[09:12] Alex Chen: hosted store raw prompts only with opt-in; otherwise we hash and store key-hash. For Dedicated/Private you control retention and we provide configuration. SOC2 and ISO docs are part of the security package.
[09:23] Marcus Lee: for pilot, we want to do a small A/B: 10% traffic with prefix-caching enabled and measure latency/P95/cost delta. can Redwood run that?
[09:30] Priya Rao: yes we can. recommend: run for 72 hours across representative traffic, we collect hit/miss and token-level savings. We'll need routing policy set to route 10% to cached-enabled subset.
[09:40] Alex Chen: timeline recap: Marcus sends corpus by 2025-06-30; Priya runs sim and returns results by 2025-07-02; Pilot kickoff week of 2025-07-07. Alex to send SOW + pricing by 2025-07-03.
[09:55] Marcus Lee: sounds good. one more question: billing nuances — do you bill cached tokens?
[09:59] Priya Rao: billing typically counts generated tokens; hits that short-circuit upstream generation still count for network/edge ops but are priced at a lower per-request fee in Dedicated/pilot. We'll include exact pricing in SOW.
[10:10] Sofia Alvarez: any recommended safety policies for prefix reuse in case of regulatory data?
[10:14] Priya Rao: if data is regulated, pin prefixes to tenant-only shards, encrypt with customer KMS, and enable strict audit logging plus shorter TTLs unless explicitly allowed. Also token redaction and PII-scrubbing in SDK before cache insertion.
[10:28] Ethan Park: ok thanks.
[10:30] Alex Chen: great — we'll follow up with the sim and pilot details. Thanks all.
[10:35] Marcus Lee: thanks, appreciate it.
[10:36] Sofia Alvarez: thanks everyone.
[10:37] Priya Rao: thanks, bye.
notes: Call ended with explicit next steps and dates; transcript has minor ASR artifacts. References: shared folder link to example prompt corpus (sent via chat), security pack (link), Redwood pilot SOW template (link).
